newsitem.title: USA: U.S. relaxes computer export curbs to Israel.
newsitem.headline: U.S. relaxes computer export curbs to Israel.

text.p: The United States has relaxed curbs on the export of advanced computers to Israel, the State Department said on Wednesday.

Under the new rules, export licenses are no longer required for computers performing up to 2,000 million theoretical operations per second, or MTOPS, a department spokesman, John Dinger, told a regular news briefing.

For more powerful units up to 7,000 MTOPS used on interuniveristy networks, "we would go into the (export) approval process presuming it would be approved," but a case-by-case review would be required, he said.

Under a policy updated by President Bill Clinton in 1995, the sale of advanced U.S.-built computers with possible military applications was restricted to countries that have not signed the treaty aimed at curbing the spread of nuclear weapons, including Israel.
The October 1995 policy provided for periodic inter-agency U.S. reviews to determine whether the restrictions on a given country were "appropriate," Dinger said.

He said said Israel was the first country to be reviewed, although he could not immediately say why. The review took place last year, he said, clearing the way for the "significantly improved" Israeli access.
